1800-10-25.journal_geographe: From noon to 4 o’clock the sky overcast, wind very variable. At 6 o’clock the wind light and variable, the sea fine, weather cloudy and humid. At half past nine we shortened sail in order to wait for the Naturaliste. Quite cool. At 10 o’clock we rallied the Naturaliste, which was appearing under the wind. From 12 to 4 weather cloudy, wind changeable. From 4 to 8 o’clock fine weather, the sea quite fair
1800-10-25.journal_baudin: On the third, in the morning [Brumaire, 25 October 1800], the sky remained overcast and the winds south by west, varying to south-west. Smooth sea. About ten o'clock the clouds began to break and we had hopes that the weather would turn very fine. During the morning Citizen Bissy took an hour angle to determine the rate of the watch in his charge, which seasickness had prevented him from attending to earlier. At noon the observed latitude was 46° 53′ north. That by reckoning put us at 47°, giving a difference of 7 minutes, the observation being further south than the reckoning. The longitude by reckoning was 12° 42′ west, and that of no. 38, according to Citizen Bissy's calculation and an observation he did not think altogether reliable, 13° 30′ 54″. In the afternoon the sky clouded over almost suddenly and the wind freshened. As there was no appearance of fine weather I signalled the Naturaliste to take a reef in the topsails and did the same myself. At half past four, the winds which had been south-west having drawn to west-south-west, I signalled to wear ship, and we steered south. During the night of the third to the fourth [Brumaire, 25-26 October 1800] the winds drew to the north-west, a strong breeze; the sea, however, was smooth for the wind. We lost sight of the Naturaliste about eight in the evening; a stern light was lit at that time and we kept the topsails on the cap to give her every possible means of closing with us. At ten o'clock the mizzen topsail had been furled and a second reef taken in the topsails, the winds having freshened. At midnight, the Naturaliste having rejoined us, I signalled her to steer south-west.

1800-10-26.journal_geographe: At half past noon caught sight of a ship in the SO 11q 0, weather cloudy, very cool wind blowing. At 4 o’clock weather changeable, a little rain falling. Very cool wind. At 8 o’clock squalls
1800-10-26.journal_baudin: On the fourth [Brumaire, 26 October 1800] the winds held north-west, a fresh breeze, and seemed inclined to settle fair, although the barometer stood fairly steady between 28 inches 4 lines and 28 inches 3, after having fallen the previous day as low as 28. During the morning we were obliged to set up our shrouds, although the sea was not very convenient for the work; but they had so much slack, especially those of the foremast, that we could not put the job off to a more favourable time without endangering the masts. We began therefore with those to windward, taking the lanyards in by a good four inches exactly measured; and when we had finished we wore ship so as to do as much on the other side. This work and this manoeuvre brought us closer to the Naturaliste, which was well to leeward of us but in plain sight. It seemed to us that she must have carried very little sail during the night to have let us draw so far ahead with the sail we ourselves had. At noon the observed latitude was 46° 53′ N and the longitude by reckoning 12° 42′ west. By an observation of Citizen Gicquel, no. 31 gave 13° 30′ 54″, that is 48 minutes 54 seconds further west than the reckoning. Citizen Bissy, being somewhat unwell, made no observation for no. 38. In the afternoon the winds were favourable and drew a little more towards the north. The sea, though smooth, became swelly, and the barometer, which rose considerably during the evening, gave us hope that the fair wind would hold. During the night of the fourth to the fifth [Brumaire, 26-27 October 1800] the wind fell away by degrees; but as we made sail in proportion, the ship went along none the worse for it. The Naturaliste was astern at a reasonable distance.

1800-10-27.journal_geographe: From noon to midnight clear weather, wind blowing in gusts, the sea rather big. We decreased sail in order to wait for the Naturaliste. At 7 o’clock we sighted a ship. From 8 to noon fine weather
1800-10-27.journal_baudin: On the fifth [Brumaire, 27 October 1800] the sky was very hazy and the weather squally, though of little consequence. As soon as the Naturaliste, which had dropped astern towards the end of the night, had rejoined us, we shook out a reef from our topsails and set the staysails. Our scientists were beginning to recover, and most of them congratulated themselves on having got off so lightly. It is true too that we had not had what is called bad weather, nor a heavy sea. At noon the observed latitude was 45° 25′ N and the longitude by reckoning 13° 40′ west. That indicated by the watches, from the observations of Citizens Gicquel and Bissy, was for no. 31, 13° 40′ 25″, and for no. 38, 14° 6′ 30″. I was a little surprised at the difference between the watches; but as Citizen Bissy was not yet steady aboard nor sufficiently used to her motion, I put it down to the hour angle he had observed. In the evening the weather turned fine, the sky cleared and the winds shifted from north towards east, a fresh breeze. Only the sea was somewhat agitated, and several of our scientists were again made uncomfortable by it. During the night of the fifth to the sixth [Brumaire, 27-28 October 1800] the weather was fine but for a few squalls of little consequence. As we had very favourable winds, the Naturaliste seemed to us to sail much better under the canvas that allowed her to carry her studdingsails than under any other.

1800-10-28.journal_geographe: From noon to 4 o’clock we steered S 33q 45’ 0 and signalled this to the Naturaliste; the weather was quite nice, cool wind and the sea beautiful. From 2 o’clock to noon the weather really lovely; the Naturaliste was not far away from us
1800-10-28.journal_baudin: On the morning of the sixth [Brumaire, 28 October 1800] the winds were north-east, a fresh breeze, and we made good way, although we often had to shorten sail to wait for the Naturaliste, which was always astern even though she carried all that wind and sea allowed to be kept abroad. The crew was employed in setting up our backstays again, which even had to be taken in hand afresh, the deadeyes having come close to meeting. At noon the observed latitude was 45° 25′ north and the longitude by reckoning 14° 35′ west. That indicated by no. 31 was found, from Citizen Gicquel's observations and calculations, to be 14° 4′ 31″, and no. 38, from Mr Bissy's, 14° 31′ 58″. The mean of these two longitudes showed that the reckoning of our run by the log had been accurate enough up to this point. In the afternoon the winds came in at north-east with light squalls; but as the barometer stood at fair, we had hopes it would not change. During the night of the sixth to the seventh [Brumaire, 28-29 October 1800] it continued to blow a fresh breeze. From time to time we had a few light squalls with rain, which did not last long and which seemed to keep the winds in that quarter of the horizon. Only the sky was more heavily clouded and overcast than usual. While we were busy taking our backstays in hand, it was noticed that part of our spare yards and masts, which I had had stowed in the main and mizzen channels, were not securely lashed, and that several spars had been damaged by chafing. All this was remedied by lashing the spare spars better and by placing chocks at intervals, so that the timber was kept clear of every hook and iron bolt in that part of the ship.

1800-10-29.journal_geographe: fine weather. At 6 o’clock sighted three ships
1800-10-29.journal_baudin: On the seventh [Brumaire, 28-29 October 1800] the winds held in the eastern quarter, from east to east-north-east, a fresh breeze, and the sky was very hazy and dark. When day broke we made out several vessels to leeward of us standing to the north. At first we thought it might be a squadron of ships of war, as they appeared to us to be in fair order and eight were counted; but on drawing nearer we saw they were merchantmen. Several showed us their colours, which were Swedish. We likewise showed ours in reply, and we passed fairly close to one another but without speaking. During the morning the sky became clearer than it had been and the weather turned fine again. At noon the observed latitude was 39° 38′ south [sic] and the longitude by reckoning 15° 10′ west. That indicated by watch no. 31 was 14° 35′ 24″ and that of no. 38, 14° 47′ 19″. In the evening we met two other vessels to windward, a brig and a three-masted ship. We passed very close to both, which showed us American colours. The sea, which we had found swelly though smooth, became less agitated, and we were making a good rate of sailing which might have been two or three miles greater had we not been obliged to wait for the Naturaliste, which was doing all she could to follow us. During the night of the seventh to the eighth [Brumaire, 29-30 October 1800] it blew a strong breeze and at times in squalls; yet the ship's speed never rose above 10 miles. I should have thought, from her build, that it ought to have been greater. I believe besides that she would need twenty to twenty-five tons more of iron ballast.

1800-10-30.journal_geographe: Fine weather; quite cool. At 2 o’clock we became aware of the two American ships, who had put up their flags; we then hoisted the French flag. At quarter to 3 we spoke to the Naturaliste
1800-10-30.journal_baudin: On the eighth of Brumaire [30 October 1800], in the morning, although we had carried little sail during the night, the Naturaliste was a great distance off, and to give her time to rejoin us we had to clew up most of our sails. The winds were then east-north-east and the sky hazy and fine. We thought ourselves very fortunate to have met with such fine weather, and to all appearances our passage from Le Havre to Tenerife seemed likely to be a very good one. The naturalists aboard, who by this time were all in good health, found this way of sailing most agreeable, and it seemed to them that the fine weather would never end, because we were beginning to find ourselves in latitudes where the sun was starting to give an agreeable warmth. The Naturaliste having closed with us, I signalled the course south-west, and we both steered on that bearing. At noon the observed latitude was 33° 20′ and the longitude by reckoning 14° 42′ west of Paris. Timekeeper no. 31 gave for west longitude 15° 0′ 33″ and no. 38, 15° 31′ 18″. In the evening the weather held fine, though the sky turned dark; but the winds were the same, and that was all we asked. During the night of the eighth to the ninth [Brumaire, 30-31 October 1800] the sky cleared again. We made no more sail than was needed to avoid drawing too far ahead of the Naturaliste, so as not to be obliged the next day either to lie almost under bare poles or to heave to in order to wait for her.

1800-10-19.journal_geographe: On 27 Vendémiaire Year 9 of the Republic [19 October 1800] we cast off from Le Havre-de-Grâce in view of an immense crowd in which each individual was sad to be losing a relative or a friend. As for me, I was leaving behind a dear fat her. We had favourable winds and our casting off went beautifully. About eleven o’clock we became aware of the English frigate which was still stationed at the entrance to the port of Le Havre and which was sailing at top speed to catch up with us; we steered towards her.2 When we were within firing range she hailed us, summoned us to lower our sail,3 threatening that if we did not they would fire on us. In fact we were so close to them at this moment that we could make out the English cannon-firers aiming for us. We immediately set about lowering the boat into the sea, and the commander got into it in order to get on board. During this time we had brought to. Some time later the commander came back on board and was followed by the captain of the English frigate and his lieutenant. The English captain walked around for a while on the bridge with the commander and then asked to see the interieur of the ship, obviously in order to reassure himself that we were not armed for war. His lieutenant stayed on the bridge and our officers having asked why, since we had hoisted the parliamentary flag, they had threatened to fire on us, he replied that they were afraid of being tricked, as many ships had used the same manoeuvre to escape, besides which they had no knowledge of our departure. Our officers having teased him a little on the lack of bravery shown towards unarmed ships, and having reproached him for the fact that they were always two or three vessels to one, he did not really know how to respond. Shortly afterwards, the English captain got back into his lifeboat, into which the commander had had some provisions placed and we immediately got back on course. The Naturaliste was quite close to us. We also saw the American corvette that had left Le Havre at the same time as us, but we lost sight of her during the night

1800-10-22.journal_geographe: From noon to 4 o’clock fair seas. Fine weather. At 2 o’clock spotted Cape Lizard from the mast head at NNE 5q 0 about 8 leagues away. From 8 to 2 heavy sea. From 1 to 2 Brumaire [23-24 October 1800] Fair seas, almost calm
1800-10-22.journal_baudin: On the thirtieth [Vendémiaire, 22 October 1800] the winds drew round about two in the morning to the north-north-east, veering at times as far as north-east. We would have profited greatly by them to clear the Channel had we not been obliged to conform to the pace of the Naturaliste, which had great difficulty keeping up with us even though we had furled our fore topsail and mizzen topsail. However, as sail had to be made to weather the Casquets, I set them along with the mainsail, meaning to wait for her once I had them at some distance to the eastward. Accordingly, at half past four I had the topsails lowered and the mainsail furled so that she might rejoin us the sooner. At half past five we sighted a large frigate, no doubt English, which passed so close to us that we were obliged to bear away to the west-north-west to avoid running foul of one another. We thought it extraordinary in such an encounter that this vessel said nothing to us; and indeed she paid us not the slightest attention and held on her course without altering in the least. She was then standing to the north with all her reefs in the topsails. About ten o'clock, the Naturaliste having rejoined us, we hoisted our topsails and made sail in company, steering west 11° 15′ south. At noon, although the weather was not very fine, we were able to see the sun and observed the latitude of 49 degrees 42 minutes north. Though this observation is a little doubtful it differs little from our true latitude, the sun having been clearly visible for three or four minutes about noon. Our astronomer, who was unwell, was not quick enough to make use of it. At the same time we saw land to the north-north-east which we judged to be Lizard Point, and it was from this last point that we took our departure. Noon bearing: Lizard Point bearing NNE by compass, 8 leagues distant, or 8° 35′ of west longitude. In the afternoon the sky again turned dark and overcast, but as it was blowing a fresh and favourable breeze I had one reef shaken out at one o'clock and the second at two, although there was still a heavy swell. It was too much in our interest to get offshore as quickly as possible to neglect making use of the weather. At five o'clock the Naturaliste being far astern, we had to shorten sail again, and she could not rejoin us until nine in the evening. The wind then began to fall, and I feared to see it settle once more in the west or south-west, the sky in that quarter of the horizon being much heavier than anywhere else. During the night the ship, labouring greatly under her tall masts, rolled very violently, and for fear of damage aloft I had tackles clapped on the backstays, which being new had a great deal of slack. The rest of the night held nothing out of the ordinary. The weather was tolerable and the winds light.

1800-10-20.journal_baudin: On the twenty-eighth [Vendémiaire, 20 October 1800] the weather was fine in the morning and the breeze very light. The winds shifted, sometimes from south towards west and sometimes from south towards east. As it was my intention to keep the sea whatever weather we might meet with, I had the cables unbent so as to have more room on the gun deck, which was greatly encumbered by the quantity of goods the crew had brought aboard at the moment of departure. Our spare spars and timber of every sort were so considerable that the guns could not be run to the ports, and we were even obliged to lash them fore and aft, there being no room to keep them athwartships. Yet in spite of all these drawbacks the corvette seemed likely to sail well, for we were often obliged to shorten sail to wait for the Naturaliste. At noon we observed the latitude of 50 degrees 1 minute north and held on our course close-hauled, the wind then being south-south-west. At three o'clock we sighted Alderney, and at four we took the following bearings: the western point of Alderney south 5° east, the eastern point south 25° east, all by compass. As it fell almost calm through the evening we made very little way, and at five o'clock the Naturaliste lowered a boat and sent across a portion of our signal rocket sticks, which had been put aboard her by mistake. By the same occasion I received from Captain Hamelin two written reports: one recording the desertion of two of his crew on leaving Le Havre, the other the discovery aboard of six persons who had hidden themselves, so that this corvette carried 125 men all told, far exceeding the number she was to have. Captain Hamelin having asked me what he should do in the matter, I told him that on our arrival at Tenerife we would decide together what course to take. After sunset the calm continued until the middle of the night, when the wind, having drawn to the west, began to blow a fresh breeze. At one o'clock I signalled the Naturaliste, which had closed with us while we lay to waiting for her, to wear ship, and we stood on close-hauled on the port tack. The advantage in sailing that we had over that vessel warned us of much time to be lost, and we judged that we would often have cause to regret that she was not a better sailer.

1800-10-21.journal_baudin: On the twenty-ninth [Vendémiaire, 21 October 1800], about five in the morning, having stood to the north-west for part of the night, a light was seen which was taken to be that of Start Point on the English coast; but this conclusion may not have been correct, and I would be more inclined to believe it was on the contrary the light of some vessel passing. Besides, the weather was not clear enough to make it out with any certainty. However, as land was thought to be seen to the north-east at daybreak, it is possible we were not mistaken. At six o'clock we went onto the starboard tack, and at nine, the weather looking very threatening, we took a reef in each topsail and struck the topgallant masts, the sea becoming heavy. At ten the winds still freshening from west towards north, we took a second reef in the topsails, and by this precaution we were made ready in good time to meet bad weather should it come on. About eleven I signalled the Naturaliste to take in two reefs likewise. During the morning a stranger presented himself to the officer of the watch, one Antoine Guth, a native of Colmar living at Mauritius. Having questioned this man on what could have led him to hide aboard, he answered that, having no means of living in France and on the point of wanting for everything, he had preferred to expose himself to whatever might befall rather than remain any longer in the destitution he was in. The interest which this man's situation inspired in me led me to place him with the purser's steward, and I gave orders that he be issued a ration like the crew. He offered besides to do whatever duty aboard he might be thought fit for, not wishing to be useless. At noon we again sighted Alderney and the rocks called the Casquets. We took the bearings given below and then wore ship, having missed stays, which did not surprise us given the state of the sea and the sail we were under. Bearings taken at one in the afternoon: the middle of the Casquets south 33° 45′ west, the easternmost point of Alderney south 20° east, all by compass. In the afternoon, the weather looking foul, I signalled the Naturaliste to close, and when she was within a quarter of a league we filled again. At five o'clock the wind having suddenly drawn to the north-north-west, we at once went onto the starboard tack, steering west 22° 30′ north, a course which allowed us to weather the Casquets. During the night the weather was fair enough, but the sea being much agitated and driven by a heavy swell from the west, the ship laboured a great deal in the pitching she underwent. The head was often buried by the sea, and one of our swivel guns to leeward was dismounted, no doubt through the fault of the borers, who had not pinned the bolt securing it to the crosspiece. As this was the first time we had met a heavy sea and the ship was truly much knocked about, all the naturalists, the midshipmen and several others of the crew were sick with seasickness.

1800-10-23.journal_baudin: On the first of Brumaire [23 October 1800] the sky in the morning was less dark than on the preceding days and the wind fell away considerably. About two in the morning it drew to the north-west, but did not stay there long. At five it seemed inclined to settle in the north-east, which gave us hope of holding it in that quarter long enough to weather Cape Finisterre. During the morning the breeze was light, and we made all the less way as we often had to lower our topsails to wait for the Naturaliste, which, although she crowded sail to follow us, always remained too far astern to be kept company with. At ten o'clock, as she appeared to be running to the west-south-west, I signalled her to close, and I steered west myself for a time so as to join her the sooner. As soon as we were within a reasonable distance of one another I signalled south 45° west, and we made sail together on that course. At noon the observed latitude was 48° 15′ 57″ north and the longitude by dead reckoning 9° 6′ west. As our astronomers were sick with seasickness, the longitude that our watches might have indicated was not observed. In the afternoon the ship laboured a great deal, the sea being heavy; and as our backstays, like all our standing rigging, were new, I had tackles clapped on all the backstays, forward and aft. During the night of the first to the second [Brumaire, 23-24 October 1800] the sky was dark and overcast and the winds very variable. We were often obliged to back the mizzen topsail and bear down on the Naturaliste to close with her, as she fell much to leeward. For the rest, the night held nothing out of the ordinary and the wind was moderate.

1800-10-24.journal_baudin: On the second, in the morning [Brumaire, 24 October 1800], it blew a fresh breeze, the winds being south, varying to south by east. The sea became smooth and only the sky remained overcast, which prevented us from observing the latitude at noon. The Naturaliste having again fallen to leeward, we bore down upon her to close. During the morning several of our scientists appeared on deck with faces somewhat undone by the seasickness some of them still had. The longitude by reckoning at noon was 10° 30′, and that of watch no. 31, from an observation Mr Gicquel was able to take in a moment when the sun appeared between the clouds, gave 9° 43′ 8″. After noon the sky remained overcast but with no appearance of bad weather. The barometer held fairly steady between 28 in. 6 li. and 28 in. 3 li., and only the hygrometer showed a great deal of moisture in the air. The winds in the evening were very variable, from south by east to south. The Naturaliste still making much leeway, we were often obliged to bear away so as not to lose her. The sea, however, was smooth enough, and the swell from the south-west, though strong, was scarcely felt. During the night of the second to the third [Brumaire, 24-25 October 1800] the winds were south by west, from which they varied little until daybreak, but the breeze was moderate. We kept a stern light burning all night to show our position to the Naturaliste, which we could not make out by eye, the sky being too overcast. That vessel likewise showed us a light from time to time. By this means we kept her at a reasonable distance to leeward.

1800-10-31.journal_baudin: On the ninth [Brumaire, 31 October 1800] we had a continuation of fine weather, only the winds had rather less force. We held on the course south 45 degrees west, always conforming our canvas to what suited the Naturaliste's rate of sailing. During the morning we saw several land larks, which came to rest on our yards. The sailors tried to catch some but could not manage it. At noon we observed the latitude, which was 31° 6′ north, and our longitude by reckoning was 15° 52′ west. That given by watch no. 31, reduced to noon, was 16° 15′, and that of no. 38, 16° 47′ west. It appears, from comparing the longitude given by the watches over the twenty-four hours, that we met with a current which set us further to the south-west than our reckoning allowed. In the afternoon we sighted a cutter ahead of us. At first we paid little attention to her and held on our course without troubling ourselves. But her manoeuvring having made her suspect to us, we judged she must be a privateer cruising in these waters. At half past four, the Naturaliste being about a league astern in our wake, the cutter manoeuvred to cut her off and board her alone, judging no doubt that this vessel, covered with sail to follow us, must be a merchantman under our escort. Guessing this privateer's intention, I at once hove to with the port tacks aboard to give the Naturaliste time to close with us before he could reach her. This manoeuvre effectively foiled the privateer's hopes, for seeing that he could no longer come at her in that way, he changed course and hove to as I had, where he remained some time observing me. In the meantime the Naturaliste having passed right under our stern within hail, I called to her to hold on her course without shortening sail, and I lay to across the wind to see what course the privateer would take. He having made no movement during the quarter of an hour and more that I lay to, I bore away to rejoin the Naturaliste. The privateer manoeuvred in the same fashion and followed me, keeping about two gunshots off. At last, at five o'clock, he hoisted English colours, which shortly afterwards he confirmed with a round shot fired to windward. We answered with our flag of truce and I hove to once more. As soon as we lay across with the port tacks aboard, he bore down within gunshot, then hauled his wind and drew off. It is to be presumed that, having seen a great many people aboard, he was daunted by the numbers and would not expose himself further. I had, however, had a boat put in the water beforehand and was preparing to send across to him had he not chosen to withdraw. As soon as our boat was in again I held on my course and rejoined the Naturaliste. At eight o'clock this privateer, having stood a board to the north, tacked again and kept in sight all night. As the weather was very fine and clear, we crowded sail to weather the Selvagens, whose latitude we reached about two in the night; by the longitude indicated by the watches, as by our own reckoning, we must have passed twelve to fifteen leagues off them.

1800-11-01.journal_baudin: On the tenth [Brumaire, 1 November 1800], in the morning, the privateer of the day before, which was about two leagues astern of us, again gave chase under various sail, but with little advantage. All morning we watched him make different manoeuvres, and so that he should not board the Naturaliste I kept her constantly ahead of me. The perseverance this privateer showed in pursuing us, despite the small advantage of his sailing even over the Naturaliste, decided me to have my guns run out to the ports, being well persuaded that as soon as he had seen our artillery he would change course, since the day before, having made out that I had none, he had not dared come aboard. Accordingly, at eleven o'clock I had the ship brought up into the wind so that he might examine us more at his ease; and a quarter of an hour later he hauled his wind and vanished in an instant. For our part we held on our course without appearing to notice his manoeuvre. The weather was very fine all morning and we had a fresh breeze from the east-north-east. At noon we observed the latitude of twenty-eight degrees forty-six minutes north, from the mean of twelve observations. The longitude, after working up the courses, was by reckoning seventeen degrees ten minutes west of Paris. That indicated by the watches, reduced to the moment of noon, gave seventeen degrees twenty minutes thirty-eight seconds for number thirty-one, and seventeen degrees fifty-three minutes five seconds for number thirty-eight, so that the latter was ahead of the other by thirty-two minutes twenty-seven seconds. Having the observed latitude, and going by the watches and the reckoning, and expecting to sight land at any moment, I signalled the Naturaliste to steer west by compass and shaped the same course myself. Half an hour later we sighted Gran Canaria, ten leagues off. Bearings at noon, the weather thick and hazy: the southernmost point in sight, south 30° west by compass. At four o'clock, the weather being clearer and the land more distinguishable, we took bearings: the middle of Gran Canaria south 15° west by compass; Punta de Anaga, Tenerife, west 11° 15′ north. After the four o'clock bearings we continued to crowd sail towards the land until nightfall, and at sunset we took a second set of bearings which gave the western point of Tenerife west by compass and the eastern point south-west 11° 15′ south. At eight o'clock, the Naturaliste being within hail, I told her we would tack at nine and would keep in the neighbourhood of the land all night on short boards, so as to be at the anchorage early the next day. The weather was extremely fine all night, there was little wind, and we passed it under topsails. At midnight the western point of Tenerife bore west 11° 15′ north by compass and the eastern point west 27° 15′ south. At the moment we sighted land, all the scientists and even most of the officers were so transported with joy that they all looked like madmen. Each called out to his comrade or his neighbour, so that an extreme confusion reigned aboard. Had a stranger witnessed what went on there without knowing of our departure from Europe, he could not have helped believing that we had just made a passage of at least six months, or that we were wanting in every necessity. Towards evening, when everyone's curiosity was rather more satisfied, each went to fetch his portfolio and pencils, and from stem to stern of the ship one met none but draughtsmen.

1800-11-02.journal_baudin: On the eleventh [Brumaire, 2 November 1800] at daybreak I signalled the Naturaliste to make for the anchorage, and for our part we did the same, hugging the coast as closely as possible so as to come to an anchor on the same board. At eight o'clock we passed the point the Spaniards call the Roquete, at nine we took the harbour pilot aboard, and at ten we let go the anchor in twenty-two fathoms in the best part of the bay. On our arrival we found seven vessels in the roads of Santa Cruz, including a large ship of the Philippines Company which was to sail within two days to carry to Gibraltar English prisoners taken by French privateers. Among the seven vessels moored in the roads were three Spaniards, two Americans and two prizes taken from the English by the French privateer La Mouche. One of these two prizes was a French vessel bound for Mauritius which had been retaken several days after being manned by an English ship. Immediately after we had anchored, the harbour master and an officer of the garrison staff came aboard to learn what the vessels were and the reasons for which they had come into these roads. Having made known to these two officers the motives of our call, they withdrew to report to the governor general. Shortly after they left I sent a boat ashore myself to pay my respects to the general and to inform the consul of my arrival. The return of the officer I had sent made known to me the favourable disposition of the Spanish governor, who, not content with what he had sent word of by my officer, sent one of his own staff to repeat that we would find with him every help and assistance we might call for. The harbour master for his part sent us an armed launch, and we moored after the custom of the country with two bower anchors, the starboard one to the SE by E and the port one to the north by west, with sixty fathoms of cable on each. Bearings of the anchorage, the ship moored and heading E by NE: the southernmost part of the mole west 30° 30′ south; the westernmost fort south-west; the easternmost fort NE by N; the great church south-west by west; the Franciscan convent west by south-west, all by compass. Latitude of the anchorage 28° 28′ 37″ N, differing from the nautical almanac by 0° 0′ 15″. In the afternoon of the eleventh I went ashore accompanied by several of my officers and by the captain of the Naturaliste with some of her officers, to pay our visit to the governor and the consul. On landing at the mole I was joined by most of the scientists, who, more impatient than the others, had pestered me ever since we anchored to let them go ashore, and to whom I had been obliged to grant it to be rid of them. I must say here in passing that those who are provided with such men, or who may be in future, should arm themselves at the outset with great patience; and I confess that although I have no lack of it, those I have have often pushed me to the limit and obliged me to retire to my cabin out of temper. Their conduct, however, being that of men who do not know the usages, must be excusable. At five o'clock we found ourselves some forty in number paying our respects to the governor, who received us very civilly and even in friendly fashion. This first visit was not made to the consul, who at the moment we came ashore was not at home. I was informed in the evening that he had been aboard the Naturaliste to look for Citizen Michaux, with whom he had been in correspondence before our arrival. After the usual compliments at the governor's we took our leave, and on parting I handed him the private letter the Spanish government had addressed to him in our favour. He repeated obligingly that this letter was not necessary to him and that everything in the island that depended on him was at our service. On leaving the governor's, the numerous company following me dispersed, and I went to the house of the harbour master, an old acquaintance of mine, and there awaited the consul's return from the Naturaliste. We met for the first time at Mr Adam's, and after the usual compliments I accompanied him to his house, where I set out the reasons for my call, asking him to procure me as soon as possible the quantity of wine I told him I needed. His answer was that he would see to it the next day and would not lose an instant in procuring it for me. He also warned me that in two days he would be sending a Spanish vessel to Gibraltar under a flag of truce to carry a hundred or so English prisoners, and that we thus had a most favourable opportunity to give notice of our arrival. The day before we came in, a small corvette of the Republic had sailed for Brest carrying the governor of Gorée, of which we had no knowledge. At seven o'clock I returned aboard, well pleased to have got through all the visits of introduction. The night held nothing out of the ordinary and the weather was very fine.

1800-11-03.journal_baudin: On the twelfth [Brumaire, 3 November 1800], in the morning, we began aboard the arrangements necessary for taking in what we were to ship at this island. The launch and the boats were put in the water so as to work more easily, and we then began to break out the hold in order to make room there for the wine. During the morning we took two hour angles aboard, the first at nine hours fifty-seven minutes forty seconds forty thirds, and the second at ten hours nineteen minutes fifty-nine seconds thirty-six thirds, true time aboard. At the same time watch no. 38 gave, for the mean longitude of these two sextuple angles, allowing for the temperature correction which is eighteen seconds in excess, zero seven of acceleration, 18° 58′ 33″ 52‴ west. According to the latest observations the anchorage of Santa Cruz lies in 18° 35′ 39″ 00. It follows that watch no. 38 gives a longitude too far west by 0° 22′ 54″ 92‴. Thus this watch has, in its rate since the fifth of Vendémiaire when it was set at Paris, an acceleration of 0° 22′ 54″ 52‴. At the same hours watch no. 31 gave for west longitude 18° 29′ 30″ 45‴. That of the anchorage being, as I said above, 18° 35′ 29″ 00, it follows that watch no. 31 gives a longitude too far east by 0° 6′ 9″ 15‴. But as there is no table of temperature correction for this watch, one must suppose that its rate would have been very regular had it been corrected on that principle. From two quadruple altitudes taken near the meridian, the latitude is given as 28° 28′ 36″ N. The nautical almanac places the latitude of the anchorage at 28° 28′ 52″; difference 0° 0′ 16″. In the afternoon I went ashore to learn what arrangements the consul had made regarding my request for a hundred pipes of wine, and I was informed that he had sent an express to the port of La Orotava and expected an answer the next day. I had thought it would be easy to find this small quantity at Santa Cruz, but the thing proved impossible, given the extraordinary quantity that had been shipped out over the past six months.

1800-11-04.journal_baudin: On the thirteenth [Brumaire, 4 November 1800] we continued aboard to break out the hold and to alter part of the stowage, which had been badly arranged at Le Havre. During the morning I had the chronometers taken ashore; and Mr Carta having had the kindness to lend me his house, on which there is a turret very suitable for observations, we had carried there such of the instruments as we might need. Although the owner of this house is a well-known man, Citizen Bissy thought that setting up the watches ashore was reason enough to take up residence there; and although we had the keys of the observatory in our own hands, he used this pretext to appear no more aboard for the duration of our call. I like to think that the result of his work will show that he will have employed part of his time in a manner satisfactory for determining the rate of the watches and useful for his own instruction. About ten o'clock the harbour master having come aboard, I was invited, as was Mr Hamelin, to the governor's house for dinner the following day. He also had his excuses made to us both for not returning the visit we had paid him, his health and the seasickness he is subject to not allowing him to come aboard. In the afternoon I went ashore, and Consul Broussonet observed to me that it would be very difficult to procure the hundred pipes of wine I had asked him for, and that should he manage to find them I must expect to pay very dear for them, since a hundred hard piastres were being asked for a very small parcel to be had at the port of La Orotava. This news was the more disagreeable to me as I had counted on finding this commodity at least at the same price as on my last voyage, and as plentiful as it was then. The English, who seem to have taken over this trade as they have that of Madeira, have driven up the price of these wines in such a way that there is today no difference between the prices of the two places, although the quality of the latter colony's wine is infinitely superior. The export of Tenerife wine is carried on quite simply in English vessels sailing from London with Admiralty commissions. On arriving in the roads they merely hoist American colours without having the papers for them. As on arrival they declare they have come to buy the wines of the country, which they say are to be carried to New England, that declaration is accepted and everyone finds his account in it. There is at present in the roads of Santa Cruz an English vessel under American colours which in three months has made two complete voyages to London without being met by a French privateer; the master of this vessel, whom everyone knows for what he is, flatters himself that this third voyage will be as fortunate as the other two, but he may well be mistaken, for the owners of the privateer La Mouche have ordered their captain to watch him closely and even to seize him if he meets him. From what the consul had told me of the difficulty of procuring wine even at a very considerable price, I urged him to make one last attempt, so that I might decide what course to take once I was well informed of the merchants' final demands. That same evening he sent again to La Orotava to ascertain positively the disposition of the wine proprietors in that part of the island. At half past six in the evening I returned aboard, as did the other members of the expedition who had gone ashore in the morning. Everyone complained a great deal in the boat of having run about all day without meeting anything of interest. The night was very fine and held nothing out of the ordinary.

1800-11-05.journal_baudin:
On the fourteenth [Brumaire, 5 November 1800], the place intended for our wine being prepared, we set about setting up our shrouds fore and aft; but as the coming and going of the boats from ship to shore and shore to ship, to carry and fetch the officers and naturalists, made me lose a great deal of time, I decided that in future they should go only three times a day, that is, in the morning at six, after breakfast at ten, and in the evening at the gun. I could no doubt have cut one of these three trips; but as the scientists do not yet sufficiently understand the drawbacks of having boats continually going back and forth, I chose to wait until experience had convinced them of the results that will soon follow from their useless excursions. The departure of the truce vessel sent to Gibraltar by the consul being fixed for the next day, I addressed the following letter to the Minister of Marine.

"In the roads of Santa Cruz de Tenerife, 14 Brumaire Year 9, aboard the Géographe. The commander-in-chief of the expedition of discovery to the Minister of Marine and the Colonies at Paris. Citizen Minister, The departure of a truce vessel sent to Gibraltar by Consul Broussonet gives me the opportunity to inform you that on the eleventh of this month we anchored in the roads of Santa Cruz de Tenerife, after fourteen days at sea counting from our departure from Le Havre. Our passage held nothing out of the ordinary, and but for a squall of twenty-four hours before we cleared the Channel we should have had fine weather throughout. The corvettes Géographe and Naturaliste have behaved perfectly well at sea in the various circumstances we have met with. I have only to regret that the Naturaliste's sailing is infinitely inferior to the Géographe's, which needs no more than her topsails and foresail to keep pace with the other when that one has, in fine weather, all the sail she can carry. As this ill is without remedy, and as Captain Hamelin has tried every means to find the greatest speed his vessel can attain, we shall get off with keeping the sea a few decades longer than if she had sailed better.

On the very day we left Le Havre I went aboard the English frigate Proselyte, which I met on my way. The reception given me by the captain commanding her was at first surly enough; but as soon as he had seen the English Admiralty passports and those of the other powers of Europe, his brusque tone softened, and drinking together to the success of the voyage we became good friends. During the rest of my passage through the Channel I met several other ships of war which appeared to pay us no attention.

The only thing infinitely disagreeable to us at this moment is our galley stoves, and to all appearances they will have to be landed. It has been almost impossible to use them, whatever means have been employed. The principle, however, seems to me sound, and the faults that result no doubt come from the execution. I enclose here a note on the most apparent imperfections of those made at Le Havre. First, all the flues for the passage of the smoke are too small and badly arranged. Second, the air they draw from the hold is not enough to make it rise. Third, it is absolutely indispensable to keep all their doors open to keep a fire in them. Fourth, at the moment when the fire is at its hottest, if they are closed even halfway it takes no more than five minutes for it to go out entirely. Fifth, the quantity of water obtained by distillation comes to no more than four pints in twelve hours; the bad taste it retains comes perhaps from the impossibility of keeping the condenser water cold. Sixth, the heat of the outer casing becomes too considerable not to give continual anxiety about the consequences that may follow. From this account it seems to me necessary that more than one trial be made of this new form of galley before its use is allowed aboard the vessels of the Republic. Even supposing that the drawbacks ours present at this moment can be remedied, I think they will still not be perfect.

Among the young men shipped at Le Havre under the name of apprentice helmsmen, three who are not and never will be fit for anything in the naval service have been landed and go by the truce vessel. I have likewise been obliged to put aboard her the master carpenter of the Naturaliste, long afflicted with a double tertian intermittent fever, and a helmsman crippled by the venereal disease; this last had evaded the inspection made at our departure. All the rest of the crew enjoy the best of health. The scientists, whose learning does not appear as extensive as their number would suggest, have been, as was to be expected, sick with seasickness, but all are recovered.

As we have not yet had time to set up our observatory ashore, I cannot tell you exactly what the error of the watches may have been since they left Paris. I do not presume it to be considerable, seeing that we sighted land at the time the watches indicated it, while our longitude by reckoning still placed us half a degree off. The consul is no doubt informing the Minister of Foreign Relations of the dispositions of the present governor of the Canary Islands with regard to vessels of the Republic that might have occasion to call in these roads. His views are not favourable, and had we been armed for war he would not have allowed us to anchor here, having, he says, orders from his court on the subject. Citizen Cossigny and his daughter have fortunately sailed for Mauritius in the very vessel that is to carry them there. I count on making sail in six days to continue my route, and I hope that the letters I shall have the honour of addressing to you from Mauritius will be more interesting than this first one. Signed N.B.

Note. By the same truce vessel that carries this letter there has been addressed to the ambassador at Madrid a case containing various kinds of seeds gathered by the gardener Riedlé and by the consul himself during his stay in this island."

At one in the afternoon I went ashore with Captain Hamelin in answer to the governor's invitation, at whose house we dined. As we found a large company there, we were informed that it was St Charles's day, the feast of the King of Spain. Had we been warned of it, the corvettes would have been dressed; but having no more saints in our calendar, we were ignorant of the one the Spaniards keep on that day, the more so as it was only an hour before sunset that three salutes of artillery were fired. In the evening, before returning aboard, I went to see the consul and handed him my letters for France. It had not been possible for him, because of the despatch of the truce vessel, to attend to our business; that ship's departure was put off to the next day, everything not being entirely ready for her sailing.

1800-11-06.journal_baudin: On the fifteenth [Brumaire, 6 November 1800] I was asked by the consul to send ashore the launches of the corvettes Géographe and Naturaliste to carry the English prisoners and their baggage aboard the truce vessel. This embarkation was carried out with great confusion, so badly was it ordered. Most of the prisoners, who had been brought from the town of La Laguna where they were held, had drunk so copiously on the way that several dropped out along the road; and those who, being less drunk than the rest, reached the place of embarkation were obliged to stay on the mole until sunset waiting for their comrades, so that our launches remained ashore most of the day. Although there were two midshipmen in each of them, that did not prevent the sailors from going off to the tavern, where, following the English example, they did not fail to get drunk like them — and we may count ourselves lucky if they took nothing worse than wine. Towards evening the truce vessel made sail with only seventy-five men of the hundred she was to carry. I put aboard her seven men from the Naturaliste and two from the Géographe. At the moment the prisoners embarked, several of them offered to ship with me, but I would consent only to taking on a carpenter to replace the Naturaliste's.

1800-11-07.journal_baudin: On the sixteenth [Brumaire, 7 November 1800] I was definitively informed by the consul that it would not be possible to procure us the hundred pipes of wine I had asked him for unless we paid a quarter above their true value. This setback was all the more damaging to me as I had been five days in these roads without having advanced at all in shipping what I counted on taking. Having reckoned up what the hundred pipes would cost me at the price the merchants wished to sell them, I should have needed a sum of seventy thousand livres in piastres, and I was very far from having that capital, the government having given me only twenty-five thousand francs for this article on my departure from Le Havre — and even out of that sum I had been obliged to take eight hundred livres to pay for various articles the administration had been unable to supply us for want of money. In this state of things I made up my mind at once and limited myself to taking only three months' drink, three quarters in wine and the fourth quarter in English beer from a prize lying in the roads. In consequence of this resolution I asked the consul to send us only twenty pipes of wine to be shared between the two vessels, and forty casks of beer, being well persuaded that I would find wine at Mauritius far cheaper and quite as good as what I should have taken at Tenerife. The consul promised me that we would have all these articles aboard the next day and that we might then sail as promptly as I wished. On returning aboard in the evening I was keenly affected by two scenes that had taken place, the first aboard and the second ashore. The one aboard concerned the manner of living there. The officers as well as the scientists did not find the mess suitable and claimed to be treated in a more distinguished fashion, wanting everything consumed to come from ashore and to consist of nothing but fish, game, vegetables, fruit and so forth — and that I should pay for all this extraordinary expense. The second, more disagreeable still, was a quarrel that had arisen between Citizen Lebrun the painter and Lharidon the surgeon. Not content with abusing one another in a manner little befitting well-bred men, they seized each other by the collar, and but for the arrival of some people from the ship there would have been a fist fight in the middle of the mole. Having assembled everyone in the great cabin, I declared formally to the officers and the others who eat at table that since the mess as it was regulated did not suit them, I made over to them everything that was aboard and that they would henceforth cater to their own fancy. I pointed out to them that although I had shipped provisions for a sum far above what the government had given me, I gave it up willingly for the sake of peace and they might profit by it; but that it was not my intention to lay out money every day to satisfy their caprices. Everyone having then begged me to continue at least until the expiry of the six months, I consented, but warning them plainly that I would change nothing in the arrangements I had made at our departure. As for the second affair, which I treated far more seriously than the first, I had the cause of the quarrel accounted for to me; and all having declared with one accord, in Citizen Lebrun's presence, that the whole fault lay on his side, I did my utmost to induce him to leave the ship; and on his refusal I placed him under arrest in his cabin, where to all appearances he will remain until we sail. I had well foreseen the drawbacks that would result sooner or later from being charged with feeding the persons embarked, whether as officers or as scientists, and it was quite against all my representations that this new method was adopted — one I fully intend not to follow when the six months I have received have expired. If, on the other hand, any regard had been paid to the observations I likewise made on the uselessness of shipping so many scientists for a voyage where half the present number would still be too many, perhaps the characters would have been better matched and I should have far less trouble. However that may be for the future, by means of the measures I have taken everything seems to have returned to the order it should never have departed from, and I hope that hereafter I shall have less cause for vexation.

1800-11-08.journal_baudin: On the seventeenth [Brumaire, 8 November 1800], first thing in the morning, I received a letter from Citizen Lebrun by way of excuse for his conduct of the day before; but my answer was that I had nothing to change in the order I had signified to him, unless he asked to be put ashore, and that on that condition alone would he be allowed to land. During the morning the consul sent us only the forty casks of beer, which I shared with the Naturaliste, and the boats that brought them promised to return in the afternoon with the wine. That same day I had various kinds of hothouse plants, which we had brought from Paris and carried this far in the best condition, taken to the garden at La Orotava. This gift gave great pleasure to the Marquis de Nava, founder of the botanical garden in this colony, and we have every reason to believe that, given the beauty of the climate and the happy temperature this island enjoys, they will do very well. I also received from Doctor Savignon at La Laguna a Guanche found some time ago in a new cavern the Spaniards have lately discovered. Being uncertain whether it was worth sending to France, I decided to examine it in the consul's presence. Having taken it out of the double wrapping in which it was enclosed, we had the disappointment of finding it in poor condition; for although the body was entire, it was too disfigured to be placed in a museum of natural history. Our examination of this corpse at least gave us a just idea of the manner in which that nation buried its dead, and we could judge, from the care it took to preserve the body from contact with the air, of the respect it must have had for them. In the afternoon the Naturaliste and I each received the portion of wine intended for us; but as it came aboard rather late, the stowing of it in the hold had to be put off to the next day. During the evening Maugé and I opened a chest I had left three years ago, during my long call at this colony, with Consul Clerget, who had apparently forgotten to have it sent to France, or perhaps had had no opportunity. We found everything in good condition; but as we knew that most such items were already gathered in the museum at Paris, we took only those that seemed to us the most curious, leaving the rest to whoever might want them. At seven in the evening I withdrew aboard as usual, and I learned that nothing out of the ordinary had happened in my absence.

1800-11-09.journal_baudin: On the eighteenth [Brumaire, 9 November 1800], as soon as it was light we began work aboard to stow in the hold the wine and beer we had shipped the day before, so as to be able afterwards to put back in their places all the articles we had been obliged to shift. This work occupied us almost the whole day, and we could not even finish it entirely. That part of the crew not employed on this task was set to taking in hand our lower shrouds, fore and aft. As our cordage was new, the standing rigging had stretched a great deal, and it suited us better to do this work in the roads than to wait until our deadeyes were altogether close together, which would not have failed to happen after a month at sea. In the course of the morning the governor, informed that I counted on sailing very shortly, sent back aboard by the harbour master the voyages of Lapérouse and of Vancouver, which he had asked me to lend him the day after my arrival. It appears, from the report made to me, that he was not pleased with what Lapérouse says in speaking of the difficulties he met with on his journey to the Peak. In the afternoon we saw two launches arrive from Gran Canaria loaded with people, and we were then told that this was part of the crew of the truce vessel that had sailed two days before. The English prisoners had seized the ship, not wishing to go to Gibraltar. According to the report of those who returned, it appears that this vessel is to make for New England, where she will perhaps have great difficulty arriving, having few provisions and making a great deal of water. All the people of the two corvettes whom I was sending back to France are among those who have come in the launches. Towards six in the evening I went ashore to announce my approaching departure to the consul and to let him know that I was waiting only for the refreshments I had asked him for and which he had promised to have delivered aboard that day. His answer was that he was expecting them from Gran Canaria and that they would surely arrive during the night, since they had not come during the day. After speaking with him I went straight back aboard, where I found the crew still at work shipping the water taken in to replace what had been consumed since our departure from France, the quantity of which was considerable enough despite the short time we had been at sea. That day another rather disagreeable little scene occurred aboard. One of my officers, much too young to be one, had since our arrival in port made the acquaintance of a Frenchman known only for his bad conduct and for various most dishonest actions. I am glad to think that Citizen Freycinet, of whom I mean to speak, had no information on the subject, although the consul had told us publicly how matters stood. At all events he invited the man to dinner, and this fellow took the liberty of bringing four other companions, so that we were at table when this new and numerous company, which I certainly was not expecting, arrived. Mr Freycinet's eagerness to receive them and to seat them at table made it plain enough to me that it was only on his invitation that they presented themselves; and I showed not the slightest displeasure, only I withdrew from the table shortly after they had taken their places. Towards evening I sent for Mr Freycinet and represented to him that he had been wrong not only in failing to warn me of the invitation he had given, but far more in having placed me at table with a man of such ill repute. I asked him at the same time that, should the like occur in future, he warn me in advance so that I might be excused from sitting at table if the company does not suit me. I hope that hereafter he will have regard to my request and that the like will not happen again.

1800-11-10.journal_baudin: On the nineteenth [Brumaire, 10 November 1800], having finished filling our casks with the water shipped the day before, I signalled the Naturaliste to take in her launch and large boat, and I did the same on my side. The rest of the day was spent restowing the ship and preparing for our approaching departure, which I hope will take place tomorrow, as we are to receive during the day the various refreshments the consul has sent to Gran Canaria for. In the afternoon, seeing no sign of the boat we had been expecting for two days, I went ashore about six in the evening to learn from the consul whether he knew anything of the cause of the delay. His answer was that he was as astonished as I that it had not yet come, but that it would certainly not be long in appearing. I resolved therefore to be patient; and as I was not entirely ready aboard, we suffered no delay on account of shipping these provisions, which were too necessary to us to be given up even had we been ready. At half past seven I returned aboard, giving orders to the astronomer, who had set himself up ashore, to bring off the next morning all the instruments I had had carried to the observatory.

1800-11-11.journal_baudin: On the twentieth [Brumaire, 11 November 1800], from early morning we went on preparing aboard for our departure, and we could have made sail at noon had our supplies from Gran Canaria arrived. At ten o'clock the harbour master came to visit us on the governor's behalf to invite us to dine with him the next day, the anniversary of His Majesty the King of Spain, if we were still in the roads. I replied to this officer that we would accept his invitation if we had not sailed, but that there was every appearance we would make sail during the night, the more so as at that very time we had sighted two boats coming from Gran Canaria, one of which was probably for me. For the rest, I proposed to go and take leave of the governor myself in the course of the day. After this first conversation the harbour master informed me that he was charged with a second commission, more disagreeable than the first, since its object was to bring me a complaint about the desertion of four grenadiers of the Altona regiment, said to have taken refuge aboard one of the two vessels. To give the governor entire satisfaction I made a most exact search aboard on the spot and in his presence, and at the same time I invited the captain of the Naturaliste to join me. Neither soldiers nor even any sign that might give grounds to suspect they had meant to come aboard was found in the Géographe. Captain Hamelin having arrived meanwhile, I made known to him the governor's complaint and the report given him that these four men were certainly aboard one of the two vessels. Captain Hamelin assured me he had no stranger aboard, and he offered, as I had done, to have the harbour master accompany him to his ship and to have the most rigorous search made in his presence. Neither of us could have gone about it better to put an end to the suspicions conceived against us, and we were ourselves too much concerned not to have four useless men aboard not to employ every possible means to verify the fact and give up these deserters if we found them. While we were engaged in this search, Consul Broussonet, his wife and his daughter came aboard, and we received them as best we could. After the first compliments the consul showed me a letter from the governor concerning the four deserters I have just spoken of. I informed him of the search I had had made aboard, as well as the one being made at that very moment in the Naturaliste. I hope, should they not be found aboard that vessel, that the governor will be quite convinced we do not have them and that the reports made to him are without foundation. At one in the afternoon I accompanied the consul and his ladies ashore, and Captain Hamelin having joined us, we dined at his house. The soldiers in question were not found aboard the Naturaliste. While we were at table, one of the gardener's boys shipped in the Géographe arrived at the consul's, covered in wounds and his face full of blood, scarcely able to stand. At first I thought he had quarrelled with someone and that the state I saw him in was the result. But as soon as he had explained himself, we had the grief of learning that, having gone ashore in the morning with the head gardener Riedlé to botanise, both had fallen from a very high rock they had climbed to get at a very rare plant or flower called Eranthemum salsoloides, which grows only on the edge of rocks and almost always in inaccessible places. The rock they had managed to climb having given way, they fell nearly thirty feet. The boy's fall was more fortunate than the other's, for he had kept strength enough to come more than a league to tell us that his companion had been left on the spot, all broken and unable to move. This accident made us all shudder at the state in which we should find Riedlé on our arrival. We left our dinner at once to go to meet him, and we took care on setting out to bring a stretcher from the hospital to have him carried to the port. The consul and Citizen Le Gros accompanied me on this occasion. Having got to about half a league from the town, we met Riedlé making his way in, supported under the arms by two men of the country who were with him. This meeting was very welcome to us in showing that he had nothing broken. When we had come up with him we had him rest and examined him. We found first a severe contusion between the nape and the occiput, a second and more considerable contusion in the lumbar region, and several wounds more or less considerable, but happily no fracture. His complexion, pale as death, showed us how much he was suffering and must have suffered from his fall. He would not, however, have the stretcher used to carry him to the port, and he made his way there with the help of the men accompanying him. When we had reached the landing place I had him taken aboard at once and put into the hands of the surgeons, who bled him a little and gave him vulnerary water. He was then without fever, his pulse only somewhat raised. This accident, befalling so essential a man, grieved me greatly; but I retain the hope that his recovery will not be long — at least that is the surgeons' opinion in the report they have made me on his present state. Before withdrawing aboard I went to take leave of the governor, who as usual received me with much politeness. He spoke to me of his deserters, and I believe I persuaded him that they are not aboard. Before letting us go he renewed the invitation he had sent me in the morning by the harbour master, in case our business from Gran Canaria not having arrived we should not sail. The light wind all day having prevented the boats we had sighted from arriving, we could not learn whether what we were waiting for was aboard them.

1800-11-12.journal_baudin:
On the twenty-first [Brumaire, 12 November 1800] our head gardener was somewhat better than the day before, having passed a fair enough night and without fever; the surgeons dressed his various wounds, and we all hope that the restoring of his health will not be very long. Two boats from Tenerife having arrived during the night, we were informed by the consul that they had nothing for us, but that the one bringing our things would without fail arrive the next day. In consequence of this declaration I decided to wait; and as that day was a great feast for the Spaniards, I gave orders to dress both vessels, which was done at eight o'clock, the hour at which the Spaniards hoisted the colours of the fortresses. In the course of the morning there came into the anchorage a prize of the privateer La Mouche, from America, laden with grain, flour and timber for London. As this vessel entered the anchorage with English colours at her main masthead, I do not think her American, although her build might give grounds to suspect it. The pilot who brought her in piloted her very badly and moored her directly over our north-west cable. I sent him a boat at once with orders to weigh that anchor immediately, failing which I would have the cable cut. A launch was at once sent for from shore to carry out this manoeuvre; nonetheless I fear that before that anchor is weighed our cable may have been damaged. At one o'clock I went to the governor's invitation, and while waiting for the dinner hour I called on the consul. On arriving I found there seven mules loaded with bananas, fruit and various other refreshments which the Marquis de Nava, founder of the botanical garden of this island, had the kindness to send me. Having thanked Citizen Le Gros, charged with offering them on his behalf, I ordered them shared equally between the two vessels and asked Citizen Le Gros to be so good as to present to the Marquis de Nava, as the only thanks I could offer him, one of the medals the government had struck for our expedition. The dinner the governor gave us was very cheerful and even agreeable. We drank to the success of the voyage and all passed off as well as possible. At the end of the meal there came up, as I expected, the question of the deserters said to be hidden aboard. I did my best to persuade the governor and the colonel of the Altona regiment, who claimed them, that we did not have them. But I had the more difficulty convincing them as a soldier in disguise, having been aboard the Naturaliste and then come ashore, declared he had seen them. As two of the Naturaliste's officers were present and affirmed that no stranger had appeared aboard, I asked that the soldier in question be sent for, to see whether he would make the same deposition in our presence. The governor would not allow it, and nothing more was said. As the boat we were expecting from Gran Canaria had not appeared, and as the threatening look of the weather made me fear being too much exposed in the roads, I went to the consul to tell him that I absolutely would not wait any longer and that I had irrevocably fixed my departure for the next morning. I asked him accordingly to send aboard as soon as possible his account of expenses during our call, and our crew lists with a note of the changes that had taken place. He promised me that all would be ready by nine the next morning and that we would suffer no delay on that score. Before leaving him I gave him, for the Minister of Marine, a duplicate of the letter I had entrusted to the truce vessel, to which I added the following.

"The Commander-in-Chief of the Expedition of Discovery to the Minister of Marine and the Colonies. By my letter of the 14th of this month I informed you of my arrival at Santa Cruz de Tenerife. The vessel carrying my packets had seemed to me a favourable enough opportunity to entrust them to; but two days after sailing, the English being carried to Gibraltar seized the ship, put the crew and passengers ashore at Gran Canaria and made sail — according to the depositions of those they landed — for the Cape Verde Islands or the coast of Africa. I leave with the consul the duplicate of the letter I had addressed to you, and I announce by this one my departure, fixed for tomorrow after nine days in these roads. The scarcity of wine and the exorbitant price to which the English have driven what remains have not allowed me to take the quantity we needed, and I judged it better to keep part of the funds you procured me in order to supply ourselves at Mauritius, where the price, whatever the scarcity, cannot but be well below this one, wine being sold here at a hundred and twenty piastres the pipe, and crowns of six livres having only the value of the piastre. Greetings and respect. N.B."

Before returning aboard I called on the harbour master to ask him not to fail to send me launches at daybreak to unmoor us, which he promised to do. Leaving him, I went to Mr Carta's to thank him for having lent us his house for our observatory, and I offered him, as a mark of our gratitude, one of our medals, which he received with great pleasure. About seven in the evening I went aboard, leaving many people still ashore, for never were the officers and others punctual in answering the gun as had been ordered. On arriving I had the satisfaction of learning that our gardener Riedlé had passed the day without fever, having suffered only the contusions that followed his fall. On the other hand the surgeons are persuaded that no serious illness will result, though they think complete recovery will be slow. During the night the breeze, which had been very strong all day, fell somewhat, but the sea remained very swelly and the ship laboured a good deal at her anchors.

1800-11-13.journal_baudin: On the twenty-second [Brumaire, 13 November 1800], in the morning, not receiving as promptly as I could have wished the launches I had asked the harbour master for the day before, I sent my boat ashore with a midshipman to fetch them. At the moment the boat left the ship, three or four of the naturalists came to ask my leave to go ashore on various matters they said they had to settle there. I refused them all this leave, the more so as, having warned them three days earlier that I meant to sail at the first opportunity, they had surely had more time than was needed to be entirely ready. At eight o'clock the launches promised to be alongside by six at last arrived, and I at once signalled the Naturaliste to unmoor. In weighing our north-west anchor we noticed that our cable had one strand cut about thirty fathoms from the clinch. This damage was caused by the vessel that came into the anchorage the day before, as I had foreseen, the pilot's bad manoeuvring having fouled her anchor in our cable. As the harbour master was aboard at that moment I had the damage attested in his presence, and I wrote at once to Consul Broussonet so that he might have the damage paid for by the owners of that prize, as they had agreed with me the day before should the cable have suffered. At half past nine the consul's clerk having come aboard to settle our accounts of expenditure, we were informed that one of the two boats in sight from Gran Canaria carried our things and our supplies, and that waiting for them would mean only a delay of a few hours. I therefore decided once again to wait, in the hope that this launch, intended for us alone, would come alongside and that we would lose far less time. To make sure of it I sent my boat off to her, but this step was useless, the master in charge of her refusing to consent. For greater vexation she went and moored half a league from us. I sent my launch to her at once so that the transfer might be made from ship to ship, and still he would do nothing, because an order was needed from the customs house, which did not come until two in the afternoon. At last, after a long wait and much ill temper, my launch came back aboard and delivered to us about half the provisions we should have had, the agent charged with procuring them at Canaria not having been able to obtain what was asked of him. At two o'clock there came aboard three seamen of La Mouche who were prisoners at Tenerife for having missed that privateer's sailing, and who asked to ship with me. I took them in place of those I had left ashore either through sickness or through incapacity. At three in the afternoon, all our business being shipped, I signalled the Naturaliste, which had likewise received hers, to get under way without further signal; and as soon as she was under sail I did the same. The winds were then north-east and the weather fine enough, the breeze coming in gusts that were often strong. Our getting under way was not done without trouble, for each of the scientists, wanting to see what was going on aboard or on the mole, got everywhere among the working parties and hampered us extremely. To restore order and avoid confusion I was obliged to ask them to keep below until we were under sail.

1800-11-14.journal_baudin: On the twenty-third of Brumaire [14 November 1800], about three in the afternoon, I made sail from the roads of Santa Cruz de Tenerife to reach Mauritius as soon as possible, much regretting the eleven days I had lost in these roads, since the reasons that had brought me there had no good effect for us; and on the contrary I have every reason to fear that most of the crew will find themselves much the worse for the conduct they kept with the women of the country, most of them infected with the itch and with other diseases more disagreeable still. In vain did I represent to most of my officers and to the scientists aboard the drawbacks that could not fail to result from their asking to be taken ashore two and more often three times a day; far from paying any heed to what I told them, they seemed on the contrary to wish to go more often, and under pretext of instructing themselves in a country too well known for there to be anything new to learn there, they came and went as one comes and goes at a fair. When I was under sail I hove to about a league from the mole to take in my boat and dismiss the Spanish launch I had kept aboard since morning. This launch was very useful to me in getting under way; otherwise I might, like the Naturaliste, have paid off the wrong way and done damage to some of the vessels lying very close to me — a risk the Naturaliste did not run, being further out and clear of them all. At five o'clock I signalled the Naturaliste to steer south-west and shaped the same course myself, carrying no sail but the topsails and foresail, while the Naturaliste had already set all her studdingsails and other light canvas. At five o'clock, the two corvettes being close to one another, Captain Hamelin let me know that he had aboard four persons not belonging to his crew. It was not difficult for me to see that the governor of Tenerife had been well informed and that those who maintained these four deserters were aboard had been quite right. I was truly vexed to learn this news; and as Mr Hamelin surely has no need of men, he might well have refrained from taking these four deserters, who, although they call themselves seamen, can be of no great use to him. I confess that had I been nearer Santa Cruz I would have had them put ashore on the spot. The governor's conduct towards us did not deserve that men should be taken from him, especially as we had no need of them. During the night of the twenty-third to the twenty-fourth [14-15 November 1800] the sky was very hazy and we had a little rain from time to time. The winds varied from north-east to east and even from east to east-south-east; it blew a fresh breeze and we made good way, continuing to steer south-west by compass. Bearings of the point of departure at five in the evening: Punta de Candelaria north 36° west; the summit of the Peak west 15° north, by compass. Further bearings at six: the westernmost point of Tenerife west 26° south; the summit of the Peak west 30° north, by compass. The fog covering Gran Canaria prevented us from sighting it.
